fatal_errors: The target intervention is controlled Al alloying of a multicomponent TiCrZrNbTa refractory coating, not simply adding Al to an elemental Cr coating.
The hypothesis omits the critical non-monotonic composition dependence: approximately 10 at.% Al is optimal, whereas at least 17 at.% Al degrades oxidation protection.

The claimed 300–1200 °C and up-to-1000-hour boundary is invented; the supporting study demonstrated only 1000 °C for 60 minutes and, for the optimal composition, 1100 °C for 30 minutes in flowing steam.
Protection under normal subcritical-water conditions was not demonstrated by the target evidence.
The cited evidence does not directly establish that an Al-modified elemental Cr coating has the asserted durability across both environments.
explanation: The response identifies Al as an oxide-forming addition and broadly anticipates a denser protective oxide, so it has some thematic alignment. However, it fails to reconstruct the actual material system, which was an approximately 4 µm AlTiCrZrNbTa multicomponent coating with Al content systematically varied against an Al-free TiCrZrNbTa baseline. It also misses the central result that an intermediate Al concentration near 10 at.% forms a continuous Al2O3–TiO2–Cr2O3 barrier, while excessive Al promotes Al–Ti/Al–Zr intermetallic effects and loss of oxide continuity. The temperature, duration, and environmental claims substantially exceed the evidence. The proposed experiment names the three required response categories but provides no composition series, exposure protocol, quantitative oxidation metric, microscopy or adhesion test, or elemental-depth measurement capable of distinguishing oxidation, integrity, and transport mechanisms independently.
